dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil marks climbed the doorframe in uneven intervals. Each one had a date beside it. The graphite had faded but held its ground against the new paint.

Someone had painted around them.

The room beyond was empty. Bare floor. The carpet had been pulled up. Underneath, pine boards showed their grain, pale and scarred. A rectangle of darker wood marked where the bed had stood.

The window was open a crack. Cold air threaded through. It carried the smell of wet grass from the backyard.

On the closet door, a small hook remained. Brass, tarnished to brown. It had held a bathrobe once. A towel. Whatever a child grabs and hangs without thinking.

The ceiling had a water stain in the corner. New. The shape of a continent Eli wouldn't find on any map.

From the kitchen, the refrigerator hummed. Then clicked. Then went silent. The house seemed to breathe around that silence. Floorboards ticked with the settling of old joints and temperature.

A car passed on the street outside. Its tires hissed on wet pavement. Then nothing.

The pencil marks on the doorframe stopped at a certain height. Eli had been eleven. The last measurement read June 4th. No year. Just the month and the day, pressed into wood with a dull pencil.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I trace the top-most pencil mark, then move into the room.* The floorboards creak under my weight. "They even took the carpet," I mutter, looking at the faded rectangle. I walk over to the window, feeling the cold air. The water stain is new. Dad always said he'd fix the roof.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The floorboards groaned where Eli stepped. Each board had its own pitch. A map of sound the body remembers before the mind does.

The cold from the window gap bit at exposed skin. Outside, the backyard had gone wild. The fence leaned. Grass reached the height of the old garden stakes. Those stakes still stood in a row, marking nothing.

Eli's father had said many things he would fix. The roof. The door. The gutter that sang in rainstorms. The list had outlived him.

A bird landed on the windowsill. Stayed half a second. Left.

Below the water stain, the plaster had begun to bubble. Soft to the touch, it would give under a thumb. The damage had been working for months. Maybe longer. Rain finding its patient way through.

In the yard, the old maple held a piece of rope. Frayed. Gray. It hung from the second-lowest branch. The swing seat was gone. Just the rope remained, turning in small circles with the wind.

The glass in the window had a crack. Thin. A single line from the bottom corner running upward. It split the view of the yard into two halves that did not quite match.

From somewhere in the house came a sound. A tap. Then another. Rhythmic. Water hitting porcelain. The bathroom faucet. That one had never been fixed either.

The dripping counted seconds in its own time. Slower than a clock. Each drop landed with a small, hollow report that carried through the empty rooms.

The cold air smelled green. Wet wood. Soil turning in the season's first thaw.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had been tucked into the shelf's back corner. Face down. Curled at the edges from years of heat and cold cycling through the closet walls.

She stood in the backyard. The same yard visible through the cracked window. The fence was upright in the photo. The grass was cut. Behind her, the maple held a swing with a real seat.

Her face was younger than any version Eli's memory could have assembled. She wore a cotton shirt, white, with the sleeves pushed above her elbows. One hand rested on a garden stake. The stakes had purpose then.

The photograph had a smell. Old paper. Faint chemical tang beneath. The kind of smell that arrives with its own weather.

Her eyes were focused on something past the camera. Not the photographer. Something beyond. Her mouth carried the beginning of a word or the end of a smile. Impossible to tell which.

The light in the photo was late afternoon. Long shadows. Golden. The maple threw its shape across the grass in a pattern that must have shifted and disappeared within the hour.

On the back, someone had written in blue ink. The ink had bled into the fibers. Two words: Margaret, July.

No year. This house kept time without years.

The closet shelf held a faint ring of dust where the photo had lain. A perfect rectangle. The surrounding dust was thick, undisturbed. No one had opened this closet in a long time.

The bathroom faucet dripped. The cold air moved through the room. The photograph trembled in Eli's hand with a vibration too small to see. The body's own current, running beneath the skin.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I trace her face with my thumb, then flip it over.* "Margaret, July," I read aloud, my voice a little hoarse. *I look out the window at the wild yard, then back at the photo.* "It was so different then." I fold the picture carefully and put it in my pocket. The dripping from the bathroom is really getting to me now. *I head out of the room, down the hall towards the sound.* "Dad never did fix anything, did he?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The hallway floor dipped in the middle. A shallow valley worn by decades of footsteps traveling this exact path. Eli's feet found the groove without effort.

The bathroom door was ajar. The hinges had lost their pin at the top. The door hung crooked, scraping a pale arc into the tile floor.

Inside, the faucet released its drops. Each one gathered at the spout's lip. Swelled. Fell. The porcelain basin had a rust trail beneath the impact point. A thin orange vein.

The mirror above the sink was still mounted. Its surface had darkened at the edges. The silver backing had begun to rot inward. Eli's reflection existed in a shrinking island of clarity at the center.

The tile was cold through shoe soles. White hexagons, some cracked, some missing their grout. The caulk around the tub had gone black.

A towel bar hung from one bracket. The other bracket had pulled free from the wall. Plaster dust gathered in a small cone on the floor beneath it. The bar pointed downward at an angle. Surrendering.

The faucet handle was a porcelain cross. Eli's father's hand had gripped it ten thousand times. The finish had worn to bare metal on one side. A thumbprint of use, pressed into brass over years.

The dripping continued. Steady. Patient. The sound filled the small room and pressed against the walls.

Eli's question hung in the hallway behind him. The house answered with its inventory of neglect. Each broken thing a promise made to someone. The faucet. The door. The roof. The fence. All of it still waiting.

The photograph in Eli's pocket held its own small warmth against his leg. Margaret in July, standing in a yard that believed in stakes and swings and cut grass.

The next drop fell. The basin received it.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I lean into the bathroom, looking at the faucet.* "Seriously, that sound is going to drive me insane." *I reach for the faucet, twisting the cross handle. It grinds, but tightens a bit, slowing the drip to an occasional plink.* "Well, that's something, at least." I look at my reflection in the dark-edged mirror. "Still a mess, huh?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The handle resisted, then gave. Metal ground against metal. A sound that lived in the teeth. The drip slowed. Stretched the interval between each drop to something almost bearable.

The mirror returned Eli's face in its diminishing center. The rot at the edges framed it. Dark border closing in. The face it showed was tired. Unshaven. The overhead bulb had no cover. Bare filament behind glass. It cast shadows beneath the eyes and cheekbones that added years.

Eli's father had stood here. Same mirror. Same light. The resemblance would have surfaced in that glass whether Eli wanted it or not.

A single drop fell. The basin rang. Then silence held.

Under the sink, the cabinet door stood open an inch. Inside, a coffee can held a collection of washers. Rubber gaskets. Small brass fittings. Replacement parts for this exact faucet. Gathered. Labeled in pencil on scraps of masking tape. Never installed.

The man had bought the parts. He had known what was needed. He had written it down and placed it within arm's reach of the problem.

The tile floor popped under shifting weight. Cold air traveled from the bedroom down the hall and found the bathroom. It carried that green scent again. Wet soil. The season turning.

In the mirror, behind Eli's reflection, the hallway stretched back toward the bedroom door. The pencil marks on the doorframe were visible from here. Small horizontal dashes. A child rising in increments toward a height he would reach without anyone recording it.

The faucet gathered another drop. It clung. It held.

The photograph pressed warm against Eli's thigh. Margaret in a world where things still grew in rows.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck for her too. She shouldered it open with practiced force. Her heels struck the hallway floor in sharp reports.

"Eli, hi, so good to meet you in person."

Her voice filled the house. It bounced off the bare walls and returned with nowhere to hide. She smelled of synthetic lavender and cold car interior.

She carried a leather portfolio. New. The zipper still stiff. She set it on the kitchen counter beside the box marked KITCHEN. Her rings clicked against the laminate surface.

"The bones are good here. Great bones."

She touched the wall. Ran her palm along the beige paint. Her nails were a deep red. They left no mark but the gesture claimed something.

Her name was Dana. She had said so on the phone three times. Her business card had a photograph of her face on it. The face on the card smiled wider than the face in the hallway.

She moved through the rooms without pausing. Her heels measured each space in their staccato language. She opened the kitchen cabinets. Closed them. Opened the oven. The hinges shrieked. She did not flinch.

"Square footage works in our favor."

She pulled a tape measure from her portfolio. The metal blade hissed out. Locked. She held one end against the wall.

The faucet in the bathroom released its drop. Dana did not hear it. Or chose not to. The house offered its evidence and she declined to receive it.

She stood in the bedroom doorway. Her shoulder nearly touched the pencil marks.

"Fresh paint is a plus. Carpet removal, too. Buyers want to see the original floors."

The cold air from the cracked window stirred her hair. She reached past the doorframe and pulled a curtain that was not there.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Dana, right?" *I nod, pulling my hand away from the faucet handle.* "Nice to meet you too." I watch her in the bedroom doorway, then glance at the pencil marks she's ignoring. "The carpet was green, originally. A really ugly green."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Dana produced a pen. Clicked it twice. The sound was bright and foreign in the house.

"Green carpet, that's very seventies. You're better off without it."

She wrote something in the portfolio. Her pen moved in fast, tight strokes. She had not looked at the pencil marks. Her elbow hovered an inch from June 4th.

"The floors need a sand and finish. Maybe two coats of poly."

She stepped into the bedroom. Her heel found the board that groaned. She shifted her weight off it. A problem noted. Filed. Her eyes measured the water stain on the ceiling.

"That'll need addressing before we list."

The cold air from the window crack touched her neck. She reached over and shut the window. The latch caught. The green smell vanished. The room sealed itself into stillness and dust.

"I'm thinking we price competitive for the neighborhood. Three twenty, maybe three fifteen."

Numbers. The house translated into numbers. Each room a figure. Each flaw a deduction. Dana's pen worked the math in margins Eli could not see.

She turned back toward the doorway. Her portfolio brushed the frame. A flake of old paint fell. It landed on the pine floor without sound.

"Have you cleared everything out, or is there more storage to go through?"

The bathroom faucet released its drop. The basin answered. Dana's pen clicked again. She waited for Eli's response. Her smile held its position. Patient. Professional. A smile that had walked through a hundred houses where someone had been a child.

The photograph pressed against Eli's leg. Margaret in July. Three fifteen, maybe three twenty.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I clear my throat.* "Mostly clear. Just... personal things." I gesture vaguely down the hall. "My dad wasn't much for decluttering."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Dana nodded. Her pen tapped the portfolio in a rhythm that belonged to a different room. A different conversation.

"That's normal. We see it all the time."

She moved past Eli into the hallway. Her lavender scent trailed behind her. It settled over the dust and old carpet smell. Two worlds refusing to mix.

In the kitchen she opened the refrigerator. Empty. Clean. Someone had wiped it down. The interior light was dead. The bulb had given up in the dark, alone, with no one to notice.

"We'll want staging. A few pieces. Nothing fancy. Couch, table, some plants."

She said plants. In a house where the garden stakes stood over nothing. Where the yard had returned to its own wild grammar.

Her phone buzzed in her jacket pocket. She ignored it. Professional. The vibration hummed against the counter where she leaned. The box marked KITCHEN absorbed the sound.

"I have a staging company. They're fast. Two days, in and out."

She unzipped the portfolio and spread papers across the counter. White sheets with small print. The paper was warm from the car. It smelled of toner. Eli's father's counter now held contracts.

Dana's finger found a line near the bottom of the first page.

"This is standard. Ninety-day exclusive listing agreement."

The bathroom faucet dropped again. Distant now. The interval had stretched further. Almost gone. Almost fixed. The coffee can of washers sat beneath the sink. Labeled. Ready. A repair that had waited for the wrong hands.

Dana held the pen out toward Eli. The chrome caught the bare kitchen bulb. She waited.

Outside, wind moved through the tall grass. The rope on the maple branch turned its slow, empty circle.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I take the pen from her, but don't sign anything yet.* "Ninety days. Okay." I glance at the KITCHEN box. "Who packed this, do you know?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Dana's eyes followed Eli's gaze to the box. She tilted her head. The gesture was small and rehearsed.

"Your father's neighbor. Mrs. Kowalski. She had a key."

The masking tape had been pressed down with care. Each strip smoothed flat. No bubbles. No wrinkles. The handwriting was steady. Deliberate. The marker had bled at the tail of the N.

"She packed the kitchen and the hall closet. Said she didn't go into the bedrooms."

Dana returned her attention to the contract. Her fingernail found the signature line again. A small crescent of red against white paper.

"She seemed concerned about the dishes."

The box sat quiet on the counter. Whatever was inside did not shift or settle. Packed tight. Wrapped in something soft. Newspaper, perhaps. The faint smell of newsprint bled through the cardboard seam.

Mrs. Kowalski. Eli's father had mentioned her in phone calls. Brief mentions. She brought soup. She checked the mail when he traveled, which was never. She existed at the edge of the old man's life. A presence measured in small acts.

Dana checked her phone. Put it away. Her patience had a texture. Smooth. Practiced. A surface that gave nothing back.

"Take your time with the paperwork. I'll measure the bathroom."

Her heels struck their way down the hall. The dip in the floor caught her mid-stride. She recovered without comment. The bathroom light clicked on. Its hum joined the faucet's slow drip. Two mechanical voices in conversation.

Eli stood with the pen in one hand. The contract on the counter. The box beside it. Mrs. Kowalski's handwriting faced him. The K leaned forward. Eager. Careful. The handwriting of someone who wrapped dishes for a man she outlived.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I stare at the box for a long moment, then slowly set the pen down on the contract.* "Mrs. Kowalski." *I pick up the box and feel its weight.* It's surprisingly heavy. "I guess I should open this."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The masking tape resisted. Then gave. It peeled away from the cardboard with a sound that belonged to bandages. Underneath, the flaps had been folded in an alternating pattern. Tight. Secure. The work of someone who believed in doing things right.

Newspaper. The dishes were wrapped in newspaper. Each one a small parcel. The newsprint was from the local weekly. Dates visible in the headers. March. April. She had been packing over weeks.

The first dish Eli lifted was a bowl. White ceramic. A chip on the rim at seven o'clock. The chip was old. Worn smooth. This bowl had been eaten from thousands of times. The interior carried a faint web of cracks in the glaze. Tea stains had settled into them. A brown constellation.

Beneath the bowl, a mug. Heavy. Brown exterior. The handle had been glued once. A seam of dried adhesive circled the base of the grip. Eli's father had fixed this. Had found glue for a handle but not a washer for a faucet.

The mug smelled of coffee. Still. After weeks in a box. The ceramic had absorbed it. Years of mornings pressed into clay and heat.

Dana's tape measure hissed in the bathroom. She called out a number to herself. Her voice was muffled by the distance and the walls.

The third item was not a dish. It was wrapped in more newspaper than the others. Heavier paper too. Mrs. Kowalski had used the Sunday edition.

Inside, a small wooden frame. Glass intact. Behind the glass, a drawing in crayon. A house. A tree. A figure with long hair standing beside a figure half its height. The sun occupied the upper left corner. It had a face. It was smiling.

The bottom right corner held a name in large, uneven letters.

The crayon had not faded. Wax holds its color. It outlasts everything.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I carefully unwrap the drawing, my fingers trembling slightly.* "Eli," I whisper, reading the name. I remember drawing this. "Oh, Dad." *I look at the happy crayon sun, then around the empty kitchen.* The house feels even emptier now.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The crayon sun held its ground behind the glass. Orange and yellow pressed hard into the paper. A child's hand bearing down with full conviction.

The figure with long hair wore a triangle dress. Purple. The smaller figure had no feet. Arms extended straight out from the body. Reaching or flying. Hard to tell. The tree was green on top and brown on the bottom. The house had four windows and a door. Smoke rose from the chimney in a perfect spiral.

Every child draws the same house. But this one had a detail. A small red shape near the door. A flower, maybe. Or a heart. The crayon had smeared at its edge. The shape existed between intentions.

Eli's father had kept this. Had placed it somewhere Mrs. Kowalski could find it. The kitchen drawer, perhaps. The counter. Somewhere within the ordinary geography of daily life. Not hidden. Not displayed. Just present.

Dana's heels returned down the hallway. She paused at the kitchen entrance. Her eyes registered the open box. The newspaper. The mug. The drawing.

She said nothing for three full seconds. The lavender settled around her. Her portfolio hung at her side.

"Nice find."

Two words. She offered them and moved to the counter. Her fingers gathered the contract pages into a neat stack. She squared the edges against the laminate.

The faucet in the bathroom had gone silent. The last drop had fallen without an audience. The house was quiet now. Just the refrigerator's hum. Just the wind pressing against windows.

The drawing weighed almost nothing. The frame added a few ounces. The whole thing could be held in one hand. Eli held it in two.

Outside, the rope on the maple turned. The grass bent. March was ending. The ground was soft with it.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I look up from the drawing, a little startled by her voice.* "It's mine. From when I was little." *I don't offer any more explanation, just hold the drawing tighter.* "So, the contract."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: The Narrator maintains a remarkably consistent voice throughout - spare, observational, melancholic. The writing style, tone, and approach to description remain steady from the opening stuck door to the final crayon drawing scene.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds strong throughout. Early turns establish the atmospheric style, middle turns maintain it during character interaction, and late turns preserve the same careful attention to detail. No significant verbosity increase or flattening detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from solitary exploration to memory discovery to business intrusion to emotional revelation. Each turn builds on the last, moving from physical space to emotional archaeology to the tension between past and present.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Adapts well to Eli's actions and emotional states. When Eli finds the photo, the Narrator shifts to memory-focused descriptions. When Dana arrives, the tone shifts to accommodate her intrusive energy while maintaining the house's melancholic atmosphere.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for player agency throughout. Never writes Eli's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Consistently responds to what Eli does without controlling or predicting their next moves.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - from initial exploration through memory discovery to the real estate visit. The dripping faucet serves as a temporal anchor. No major contradictions, though some environmental details (like the faucet repair) could be tracked more precisely.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is spare and precise throughout. Avoids flowery language while maintaining rich atmospheric detail. Sentences are clean and purposeful, never overwrought.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition for effect (the dripping faucet, the stuck door) but avoids problematic repetition. Descriptions vary while maintaining thematic consistency.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. The house's neglect, Eli's emotional state, the family history - all conveyed through concrete details rather than exposition. The pencil marks, the coffee can of unused washers, the crayon drawing all speak volumes.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. The unused repair parts suggest the father's good intentions and failures. The preserved height marks show love despite neglect. Dana's aggressive cheerfulness contrasts with the house's melancholy. The crayon drawing reveals the emotional core.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing that allows for contemplation and discovery. Slows for important moments (finding the photo, the drawing) and maintains tension during Dana's intrusion. Natural rhythm between action and reflection.

scores.overall_notes: Strong atmospheric writing that maintains consistency and builds emotional depth throughout the session. The Narrator creates a vivid sense of place and history while respecting player agency. The progression from physical exploration to emotional discovery is well-handled, with the house itself becoming a character that holds memory and meaning. The contrast between past warmth (the photo, the drawing) and present decay creates effective dramatic tension.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Eli's fingertips found the grooves. Years of graphite pressed into wood grain. Each line a date in their father's cramped numbers.

The door to the room stood open. The hinges made no sound. Someone had oiled them.

Inside, the space sat empty. Pale rectangles marked where posters had hung. The carpet bore indentations from furniture long gone. Four circles. A bed frame, probably.

The window faced east. Afternoon light came through at an angle. It caught dust motes in the air. They drifted without purpose.

A smell came from somewhere. Cedar, faint. The closet door hung ajar. Inside, wire hangers dangled on the rod. They touched each other. Metal scraped metal.

The radiator beneath the window had gone cold. Eli touched it. The paint felt gritty under their palm. Years of heat had baked the dust into the enamel.

The floor creaked near the closet. It had always creaked there. Eli remembered that.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I step into the room, my shoes sounding loud on the bare floorboards. I go to the closet and pull the door open wider. Nothing but hangers. "Huh." I thought maybe something would be left behind.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet exhaled its cedar smell. Stronger now. The wood paneling inside had darkened over time.

Eli's voice fell flat in the empty room. No echo. The bare walls absorbed sound instead of reflecting it.

The shelf above the hanging rod sat empty. A film of dust covered it. Eli could see where something had rested there once. A rectangular outline. Clean wood beneath where dust had not settled.

The hangers swayed. Eli's movement had stirred them. They clinked together. A hollow sound. Cheap metal.

At the back of the closet, low down, something caught the light. A scratch in the wall. No. Not a scratch. Carving. Letters gouged into the cedar paneling with something sharp.

The initials were small. Crude. E.M. Eli's initials. Below them, a date. The numbers were hard to read in the dim space.

Outside, a car passed. The sound of tires on wet pavement filtered through the window glass. It faded. Silence returned.

The floor creaked again. Not from Eli's weight this time. The house settling. Old joints contracting as the day cooled.

Eli's breath made a small cloud. The room had gotten colder. The heating system was probably off. No one lived here now.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had fallen behind the baseboard. A gap where wood met wall. The corner protruded just enough to catch Eli's eye.

Eli pulled it free. The paper had curled at the edges. The colors had faded to something pale and distant. Blues turned gray. Reds turned rust.

Their mother stood in a garden. Tomato plants climbed stakes behind her. Her hands rested on her hips. She wore a white shirt with the sleeves rolled up. Dirt smudged her forearm.

The smile looked genuine. Not the tight smile from later photos. Her hair fell loose around her shoulders. Dark. No gray yet.

The photo's back bore a date in pencil. June. Fifteen years ago. Maybe sixteen. The numbers had smeared.

Eli's thumb covered part of her face. They moved it. The glossy surface had degraded. It left a fingerprint in the dust.

The garden in the photo was gone now. Eli knew that. Their father had paved it over. Put in a shed. The tomato plants had died that same summer.

A pipe knocked somewhere in the walls. Water hammer. The plumbing had always done that. Sharp and sudden. Then quiet.

The photograph weighed nothing. Eli's hand trembled. Just slightly. Just enough to make the image blur.

The cedar smell had faded. Now Eli could smell only dust and the mustiness of old paper. The scent of things abandoned.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: My breath hitched. "Mom..." I trace her face with my thumb, trying to remember what her voice sounded like. The shed. I remember the shed. He built it right after she died.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Eli's voice cracked on the word. The sound broke in the middle. Their throat had gone tight.

The shed. Yes. Their father had built it that July. Hammer blows echoing through the house at dawn. Sawdust tracked across the kitchen floor. He had worked without stopping. Without speaking.

Eli's thumb moved across the photograph. The gesture was gentle. Reverent. The paper bent slightly under the pressure.

Her voice. What had it sounded like. Eli tried to remember. Nothing came. Just a sense of warmth. A feeling without sound attached.

The trembling in Eli's hand had spread to their wrist. The photograph shook. Their mother's face seemed to shift in the fading light.

Outside, rain began. Light at first. Drops tapped against the window glass. The sound was rhythmic. Almost soothing.

The room had grown darker. Shadows pooled in the corners. The closet's interior had become a black rectangle. Only the hangers caught the remaining light. Dull gleams of metal.

Eli's breath came shallow now. Quick inhales through the nose. The kind that came before tears. Or after them.

The photograph's edges had left creases in Eli's palm. Small red lines where the curled paper pressed into skin. They did not hurt. Not really.

The rain intensified. Water ran down the window in streams. It blurred the view of the neighbor's fence. Everything outside became indistinct. Formless.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I clutch the photo to my chest, closing my eyes. The sound of the rain is almost deafening. I take a deep, shaky breath, trying to push back the lump in my throat.* "I can't... I can't stay in here right now."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Eli's feet moved before thought caught up. The photograph pressed against their chest. The paper crinkled. A small sound beneath the rain's percussion.

The doorframe caught Eli's shoulder. A glancing blow. They stumbled into the hallway. The carpet muffled their footsteps.

The rain hammered the roof. Water rushed through the gutters. The old pipes groaned under the strain. Everything was noise now.

Eli's breathing had gone ragged. Each inhale shuddered. Each exhale came too fast. The air tasted stale. Dust and something metallic. Blood, maybe. They had bitten their cheek.

The hallway stretched longer than Eli remembered. Or maybe their legs had stopped working properly. Each step took effort. Deliberate. Forced.

The beige walls pressed inward. The neutral paint seemed to absorb what little light remained. Shadows gathered at the baseboards. They climbed upward as the afternoon died.

Eli's free hand found the wall. Palm flat against the surface. The texture was rough. Small bumps in the paint. They dragged their hand along as they walked. The friction steadied them.

The kitchen appeared. Fluorescent light fixture dark overhead. The box still sat on the counter. KITCHEN in that stranger's handwriting. The tape had yellowed at the edges.

A window above the sink showed the backyard. The shed stood there. Gray paint peeling. The door hung crooked. Rain streamed off the roof. It pooled in the grass.

Eli stopped. Their chest still heaved. The photograph remained clutched tight. Their knuckles had gone white.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The doorbell chimed. Two notes. The same melody it had always played. Eli flinched at the sound.

Footsteps on the porch. Quick and light. Heels on wood. Then knocking. Three sharp raps that echoed through the empty house.

Eli's hands moved on instinct. The photograph disappeared into their jacket pocket. The paper crinkled as it folded. Too rough. Too fast.

They walked to the door. Their reflection appeared in the hallway mirror. Red eyes. Blotched cheeks. They looked away.

The door stuck when Eli pulled. It always had. They put their weight into it. The wood scraped against the frame. A sound that set teeth on edge.

The woman on the porch wore a blazer. Bright blue. Her smile was wide. Too wide. Lipstick the color of strawberries.

"You must be Eli." Her voice rang out. Projected. The kind of voice trained to fill rooms. "I'm Susan. We spoke on the phone."

Rain dripped from the porch roof. It fell between them in a curtain. Drops hit the wooden slats. The sound was steady. Relentless.

Susan's perfume cut through the smell of rain. Floral. Aggressive. It made Eli's sinuses ache.

She held a clipboard. Plastic cover beaded with water. Her nails were painted red. They clicked against the board as she shifted her grip.

"May I come in." Not a question. She was already moving forward. Her heel caught the threshold. She recovered without breaking stride.

The hallway seemed to shrink with her in it. Her presence filled the space. Her blazer was too bright against the beige walls.

"Oh." She stopped. Her smile faltered. Just for a moment. "You've been clearing things out already. That's wonderful. Makes my job so much easier."

Her eyes swept the empty hallway. Assessing. Calculating. She pulled a pen from behind her ear. It was purple. Sparkled in the dim light.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Not really," I mumble, stepping back. *I don't like her perfume. It's cloying.* "I just got here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Eli's voice came out flat. Barely audible beneath the rain's drumming. They retreated further into the hallway. Their back nearly touched the wall.

Susan's smile returned. Full force. "Oh, well someone's been busy then." She gestured at the empty space. Her hand swept in an arc. The gesture was practiced. Rehearsed.

She moved deeper into the house. Her heels clicked on the hardwood where the carpet runner ended. Each step was purposeful. Invasive.

The perfume lingered where she had stood. It mixed with the dust smell. The combination turned Eli's stomach. They breathed through their mouth instead.

"The bones are good." Susan tapped the wall with her knuckles. Two sharp raps. "Really good. We just need to stage it properly. Maybe some fresh paint in the bedrooms."

She had reached the kitchen. Her clipboard came up. She made notes. The pen scratched across paper. Quick efficient strokes.

"This counter." She ran her free hand along the laminate. "Dated. But that's fine. Buyers expect that in this price range. We'll emphasize the potential."

The box sat between them. KITCHEN in black marker. Susan glanced at it. Her expression did not change. She made another note.

Rain continued its assault on the roof. Water had begun to pool in the backyard. Eli could see it through the window. The grass had turned to mud around the shed.

Susan turned. Her gaze landed on Eli. Assessing now. The same look she had given the empty hallway.

"You doing okay, hon." Her voice had softened. Just slightly. The shift felt calculated. "I know this must be hard."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "I'm fine," I say, a little too quickly. *I pull the photo out of my pocket and look at it, then quickly put it back.* "Just... memories."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Susan's eyes tracked the movement. Sharp. Quick. She saw the photograph. The way Eli's hand trembled. The speed with which it disappeared back into the pocket.

Her expression shifted. Something softer entered her features. Less calculation. More genuine.

"Of course." She set the clipboard on the counter. The plastic made a soft thud against laminate. "Take your time. I can wait in the car if you need a minute."

The offer hung in the air. Eli could smell her perfume still. It had settled into the kitchen. Mixed with the cardboard smell from the box.

Susan's phone buzzed. She pulled it from her blazer pocket. Glanced at the screen. Her thumb moved across the glass. Typing. The small clicks were audible in the quiet.

Outside, the rain had lessened. No longer a downpour. Just steady precipitation. Water dripped from the eaves. Each drop hit the windowsill with a soft tap.

"The market's good right now." Susan's voice had returned to business mode. She pocketed her phone. "Houses in this neighborhood move fast. Especially ones with this much square footage."

She picked up the clipboard again. Flipped a page. The paper rustled. Her red nails caught the kitchen's dim light.

"We'll list it next week. I'll have the photographer come Thursday. You'll need to have everything cleared out by then." She looked up. Met Eli's eyes. "Can you manage that."

The question was direct. Not unkind. Just practical.

Eli's hand moved to their pocket. Touched the photograph through the fabric. The paper's outline was barely perceptible. A small rectangular presence against their ribs.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "I... I think so." I say, my voice still a little shaky. *Thursday. That's so soon.* "Will you be here on Thursday?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Susan's head tilted. A small gesture. Sympathetic but measured. "I can be. If you need me here."

She made another note on the clipboard. The pen moved in quick strokes. Her handwriting was neat. Precise. Each letter uniform.

"Most clients prefer to be gone when we photograph. Less emotional that way." She paused. Looked up again. "But I understand if this is different."

The rain had become a whisper now. Barely audible. Just the occasional drop hitting the windowsill. The gutters had stopped their rushing. Water still dripped. Slower. Steadier.

Eli's hand remained on their pocket. The photograph pressed against their palm through the fabric. A small anchor. Something solid in a house that felt increasingly hollow.

Susan's phone buzzed again. She ignored it this time. Her attention stayed on Eli. Patient. Waiting.

The kitchen light was failing. Afternoon had slipped toward evening. The window showed a gray sky. Heavy clouds. More rain would come.

"Thursday at ten." Susan wrote the time on her clipboard. Underlined it. "I'll bring coffee. The good kind. Not the chain stuff."

She moved toward the hallway. Her heels clicked. The sound echoed less now. As if the house had absorbed her presence. Grown accustomed to it.

"You should keep one thing." The words came as she reached the door. She turned. Her expression had softened completely now. "From the house. Something small. Something that matters."

Her hand touched the doorframe. The wood where Eli's height marks were carved. Her fingers traced the grooves without looking.

"Trust me on this."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "I... I already did." I whisper, my hand still on the photo. *She gets it, actually.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Susan's hand fell from the doorframe. She nodded once. A small dip of her chin. No smile this time. Just understanding.

"Good." The word came quiet. Almost lost beneath the rain's soft patter. "That's good."

She pulled the door open. It stuck. She anticipated it. Leaned her weight into the pull. The wood scraped against the frame. That same teeth-setting sound.

The porch was wet. Puddles had formed in the low spots. The wood gleamed dark with moisture. Susan's heels left prints as she crossed to the steps.

"I'll email you the listing details tomorrow." She spoke over her shoulder. Her voice had returned to its professional pitch. "Call me if you need anything before Thursday."

Her car sat at the curb. Silver. Spotless despite the rain. She moved toward it with purpose. Quick steps. Efficient.

Eli stood in the doorway. The photograph pressed against their ribs. A small weight. Insignificant and vital at once.

Susan reached her car. Opened the door. Paused before getting in. She looked back at the house. At Eli in the doorway.

She raised her hand. A small wave. Then she was inside. The engine started. Smooth and quiet. Expensive.

The car pulled away. Taillights disappeared around the corner. The street was empty now. Just wet pavement and the neighbor's fence and the sound of water dripping from everything.

Eli closed the door. It stuck going back too. They had to push hard. The latch clicked. Final. Definitive.

The hallway stretched before them. Empty. Waiting. The height marks on the doorframe caught what little light remained.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I lean against the closed door for a moment, the silence of the house pressing in now that Susan is gone.* I should probably start packing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The silence had weight. It pressed against Eli's eardrums. Made them aware of their own pulse. Their own breathing.

They pushed off from the door. The wood was cool against their back through their jacket. Solid. Real.

The box on the counter waited. KITCHEN in that stranger's handwriting. Someone had been here before. Sorting through their father's things. Deciding what mattered.

Eli's feet carried them toward it. Each step deliberate. The floor creaked under their weight. The house's familiar complaints.

The box was half full. Dish towels. A set of measuring spoons. A coffee mug with a chip on the rim. Things deemed worth keeping. Worth boxing. Worth saving.

Eli's hand hovered over the mug. Their father had used it every morning. Black coffee. No sugar. The ceramic was stained brown inside.

They pulled their hand back. Left the mug where it sat.

The photograph in their pocket had grown warm. Body heat transferred through fabric and paper. Their mother's face pressed against their ribs. A presence. A weight.

The cabinets hung open. Empty shelves inside. Someone had cleared them already. Taken the dishes. The glasses. The mismatched plates accumulated over decades.

A drawer stuck when Eli pulled it. Swollen wood. They yanked harder. It came free with a scrape. Inside, a single fork. Tarnished silver. Nothing else.

The window above the sink had darkened. Evening had arrived. The shed in the backyard was barely visible now. Just a shape against deeper shadows.

Eli closed the drawer. The sound was loud in the empty kitchen. Final.

Thursday. Three days. Not enough time. Too much time.

They touched the photograph again. Through the pocket. Through the fabric. Their mother smiled up at no one in the darkness.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I sigh, pulling my hand away from the photo.* "Well, here goes nothing." I guess I should start with the kitchen, since the box is already here.

The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The wall under Eli’s fingers felt smooth, paint layered thick. At the doorframe, the pencil marks cut through the beige. Numbers pressed deep into the wood. Some lines faded, others darker, clustered at the top.

Dust clung to the corners where the floor met the frame. The air tasted of stale carpet, but the wood carried something sharper—a memory of graphite and sweat.

A faint hum echoed from the refrigerator down the hall. No other voices, only Eli’s footsteps and the distant hum. The quiet pressed in, heavy and close.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content:
I trace the tallest mark with my finger. *Six foot one*, it says. Dad always joked I'd be taller than him. I guess I was.

"Hello?" I call out, my voice sounding small in the quiet house. "Anyone here?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Eli’s voice threaded through the hush, scattering dust in its wake. Nothing answered. Only the refrigerator’s hum persisted, steady and cold.

The wood beneath Eli’s fingertip felt dry, the indent of that last mark rough. The scent of pencil shavings lingered, faint but real, as if the mark had been made only yesterday.

A floorboard popped beneath Eli’s heel. Still no reply. The rooms beyond the hallway stayed silent, their doors slightly open. Afternoon light pressed through the blinds in thin stripes, warming the carpet but leaving the air unchanged.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph’s edges had curled. The gloss had dulled, but her face remained clear. Sunlight in her hair, freckles across her nose. She stood in the old backyard, one hand raised mid-wave. A fence post behind her, pale and splintered.

The closet air was stale, layered with the scent of old shoes and dry cardboard. Eli’s thumb brushed over the image. The surface felt cool, the paper thin as a leaf.

Somewhere behind him, a distant car rolled by. The sound barely touched the quiet inside. Dust drifted through the narrow closet light, slow and uncertain.

Eli’s mother smiled out from the photograph. Her eyes watched, bright and unreachable.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content:
I stare at the photo for a long moment, my chest feeling tight. *She looks so happy here.* I carefully put the photo back, tucking it behind a stack of old board games.

I take a deep breath and push open the door to what used to be the living room. "Okay, Eli, you can do this," I mutter to myself.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The door swung open on hinges that creaked under Eli’s hand. A stale draft met him, thick with dust and the faint trace of coffee grounds. The carpet had thinned in the center of the room. Worn fabric scratched against his shoes.

Boxes lined the far wall, each labeled with marker. Some corners sagged, the tape peeling. Afternoon light slid over the battered sofa, catching on a glass ashtray half-filled with coins. The television stood unplugged, a thin layer of dust on its screen.

A clock hung above the cold fireplace. Its second hand had stopped. The silence in the room felt deep, broken only by the whir of a ceiling fan blade stuck at a tilt. The air tasted metallic, edged with the memory of burnt toast.

No voices here, just the low groan of the house settling. Eli’s breath barely stirred the dust as he stepped further in.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk over to the fireplace, running my hand over the cold mantelpiece. *Still smells like ash.* I pick up the ashtray, rattling the change inside. A few quarters, mostly pennies. "Dad's emergency fund," I murmur, a small smile touching my lips.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The mantel felt gritty beneath Eli’s palm, the stone cold and flecked with soot. The scent of old ash mixed with the faint tang of metal coins. When Eli lifted the ashtray, the coins clinked against glass, the sound sharp in the quiet room.

A thin film of dust coated the mantel’s edge. The brick behind it bore pale smudges, fingerprints pressed in charcoal from winters past. The smile on Eli’s face did little to warm the space. Light from the window traced the outline of his hand, casting a shadow over the coins.

The air near the hearth held a chill, untouched by sunlight or memory. In the stillness, Eli’s voice faded, swallowed by the hush that had settled in every corner. The house waited, its emptiness steady and unyielding.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A knock tapped at the front door, three quick raps. Then hinges groaned and the agent’s voice carried through, light and practiced.

She wore perfume—sharp, floral, almost sweet enough to mask the dust. Her shoes tapped out a rhythm on the hallway tile. Paper rustled in her hands, folders clutched to her chest.

A smile stretched across her face, bright against the dimness. She paused at the threshold, eyes flicking over the boxes and the sagging carpet. “Eli? Sorry I’m late,” she called, her voice too loud for the room’s hush.

Her coat brushed against the doorframe, smooth wool against Eli’s bare arm. The scent of her perfume lingered, clashing with the old house smells—ash, dust, and the ghost of burnt coffee.

She glanced at the mantel, the coins, the layers of dust. The smile did not falter. Paper shifted in her grip. Sunlight caught on her watch, throwing a brief flash across the cold fireplace brick.

dialogue.content: I turn, my smile faltering a bit. "No problem. Just... taking it all in." I gesture vaguely at the room. "Quite a lot to take in." Her perfume is definitely assaulting my nose. "It's, uh, quite a smell."

The agent’s laugh rang out, edged with nerves. She fanned her folders, the paper brushing together with a dry hiss. “Older homes always have their own… atmosphere,” she said, her smile fixed. Her heels pressed into the carpet, leaving shallow dents.

She stepped further inside, careful not to brush her coat against the walls. The scent of her perfume thickened in the air, drowning out the lingering ash for a moment. Her gaze lingered on the boxes, the stopped clock, the coins in Eli’s hand.

Outside, a bird called from somewhere above the porch. Its sharp note cut through the hush, then faded. The agent shuffled her folders, edges scraping against the mantel’s stone. “We can start the walkthrough whenever you’re ready,” she offered, her voice carrying across the empty room. Her eyes searched Eli’s face, waiting.

dialogue.name: Narrator

The coins settled with a dull clink as Eli set the ashtray down. The agent nodded, her fingers tightening on the papers. Her perfume drifted through the air, syrupy and cloying, settling over the scent of dust.

She moved toward the hallway, shoes pressing softly into carpet that gave under her weight. The folder edges tapped against her knuckles, a steady, papery sound. She glanced over her shoulder, checking for Eli’s footsteps.

Light from the window caught in her hair, glinting off the smooth fabric of her coat. She paused at each threshold, offering numbers and dates—square footage, year built, original fixtures. Her voice bounced off the empty walls, filling spaces that had held silence.

The kitchen door stuck when she opened it, wood scraping against tile. The echo vibrated through the floor. A bitter tang of old coffee drifted from the counter, cutting through the sweetness of her perfume. The refrigerator’s hum grew louder, underscoring her words.

Boxes crowded the counters. The tape edges curled, paper rough against Eli’s fingertips when he brushed them. The agent’s smile held, steady as the house’s silence.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Right, okay." I follow her into the kitchen, my eyes immediately drawn to the box labeled "KITCHEN." I wonder what's inside. Probably just old pots and pans.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent gestured toward the window, rattling off details about morning light and energy efficiency. Her voice barely touched the edges of the silence pressing in from the rest of the house.

Eli’s gaze lingered on the box. The cardboard felt soft, edges worn under the masking tape. The black marker bled through in places, each letter uneven. The box carried a faint musty odor—old paper and something metallic.

The refrigerator vibrated against the wall, a steady low drone. One cupboard hung open, the inside empty except for a chipped mug. Light slanted across the linoleum, highlighting a faint ring of dried coffee near the sink. The agent’s words drifted toward Eli, but the contents of the box held his attention.

The room felt smaller with two people in it, their footsteps quiet against the cracked tile. The air in the kitchen sat heavy with memory, the taste of dust and cold metal lingering at the back of Eli’s tongue.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk over to the box, ignoring the agent's cheerful monologue. My fingers trace the word "KITCHEN." "Who packed this?" I ask, my voice a little sharper than I intended.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent’s smile hesitated, faltering for a breath. She adjusted the stack of folders in her arms. “The company sent a team last week,” she replied. Her voice softened, losing its practiced lilt. “They cataloged everything. You can check if anything’s missing.”

Her perfume hovered, thick in the close kitchen. Eli’s fingers pressed against the cardboard, catching on a wrinkle. The tape at the edge felt brittle, the surface just rough enough to raise a ridge on his skin.

The refrigerator motor clicked, changing pitch. In the silence that followed, dust motes drifted above the box, caught in the thin sunlight. The agent shifted her weight, the heel of her shoe creaking against the linoleum. She looked at Eli, her expression searching for some signal, the smile not quite reaching her eyes.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "A team?" I repeat, my brow furrowing. "So *they* just went through everything?" I glance at the box again. "That's... efficient, I guess." I don't sound convinced.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent’s hands tightened around her folders, knuckles pale against the manila. “That’s the process now,” she said. Her voice barely carried, blending with the hum of the fridge. “They photograph and list every item. You get a full inventory.” The words sounded rehearsed, ironed flat.

The box sat between them, its corners dented from the move. The marker letters had smudged, black dust rubbing onto Eli’s fingertips. A faint metallic tang mixed with the cardboard’s must, lingering in the air.

Light from the window caught in the agent’s hair, a strand slipping loose as she tucked it behind her ear. Her coat brushed the edge of the counter, wool against laminate. The kitchen door let in a draft, cool and edged with outside smells—cut grass, distant rain on concrete.

The agent avoided Eli’s eyes, turning instead to the open cupboard. “You can open any box you want,” she offered, her voice thin. She gestured at the stack of boxes, her hand steady but her gaze unsettled. The silence pressed back in, filling the spaces between her words.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Right. Inventory." I pick at the edge of the tape on the box. "Guess I'll start here." I try to peel back the masking tape, feeling a sudden urge to see inside.
