Maren’s years of tending the Antler had given her an instinct for the currents that moved through her walls at night — the creak of stair treads, the shifting weight of dreams, the restless footsteps of those too troubled to sleep. Though she’d retired to her own small quarters just past midnight, the habits of a quartermaster and a tavern-keeper both ran deep. She slept lightly, always listening for what did not belong.

So when the hush of the hour was disturbed — the subtle tension in the timbers above, the faintest echo of someone stirring in Room 7 — Maren woke without alarm or hurry. She slipped the silver ring back onto her left thumb, pulled her leather apron over her shoulders, and moved to the foot of the stairs. There, she waited, listening: the night offered only the soft tick of the clock in the common room and the slow, steady breath of a house at peace.

She ascended the first few steps with deliberate quiet, pausing just below the landing, out of sight but within easy earshot of Traveler’s door. She did not intrude or call out — she knew better than to rattle a guest already uneasy. Instead, she let her presence be a quiet anchor in the dark, the solid weight of someone awake and attentive.

If trouble brewed — real or imagined — Maren would be there. She kept her left hand tucked casually at her side, but the old oak cudgel hung just behind her apron’s hem, ready if the night demanded more than words.

She waited, breathing in the cool scent of the old wood and listening for the signal she always honored: a knock, a call, or even the sound of the latch. Until then, she kept watch, steady and silent, the guardian of peace in the small hours before dawn.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I slowly get out of bed, careful not to make a sound. I pick up the package, holding it close, and tiptoe to the door. I press my ear against it, listening.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: Maren nodded. She put down her rag, her movements economical and precise. "You have chosen well, friend. Old Pell's venison stew is the special tonight, and it is indeed hot. For a room, I have several available. They are clean and quiet. Twelve silver for the night, food not included." She paused, her gaze steady. "Will that be acceptable?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, digging into a pouch at my belt.* "That'll do fine. Stew sounds good." *I pull out a few coins and slide them across the bar.* "And a mug of whatever's on tap, if you please."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the Traveler’s movements, her eyes noting the way they handled their coin pouch. She picked up the offered coins with her left hand, her fingers swiftly counting them. “Excellent,” she said, confirming the amount. She then turned, still using her left hand, to draw a mug of ale from the tap. The amber liquid flowed smoothly, topping the mug with a frothy head. She slid the mug across the polished bar towards the Traveler.

“Your room key will be ready once you have finished your meal,” she informed them, her voice calm and even. “Old Pell will have your stew out directly.” She then returned to her tally sheet, though her attention remained subtly on the common room, as it always did.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren's eyes narrowed ever so slightly as the plate was set before them. Her gaze flickered to the merchant, then to the Traveler, and finally to the offending dish. A faint flush rose on her neck, but her expression remained otherwise unreadable.

"My sincerest thanks to Lord Havel," Maren said, her voice a little stiffer than before, but still polite. She did not reach for the crab cakes. Instead, she pushed the plate gently, using the back of her left hand, a few inches away from her side of the bar. "However, I do not care for seafood, friend. It is an acquired taste, and one I have never managed to acquire." She offered a small, tight smile that did not quite reach her eyes. "Perhaps our guest would enjoy a double portion."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow at Maren's reaction, then look at the crab cakes.* "Oh, well, that's a shame. More for me then, I suppose." *I pick one up, examining it before taking a bite.* "These are actually quite good."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: Maren simply nodded, her gaze fixed on the Traveler as they ate the crab cake. Her expression remained neutral, but there was a subtle tension in her shoulders. She did not comment on the Traveler’s enjoyment of the dish. Instead, she picked up her rag once more, continuing to wipe down the already clean bar, her movements a little more deliberate than before. She kept the plate at arm's length, making no move to remove it from the bar, but also ensuring she would not accidentally brush against it.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: Maren allowed a small, genuine smile to touch her lips. “Old Pell will be pleased to hear that, friend. He takes great pride in his stew. I will be certain to tell him.” She raised her own mug in a silent, brief toast to the invisible cook, then took a measured sip of her ale. Her gaze lingered on the Traveler for a moment, a hint of warmth in her eyes. “He says the secret is patience, and good quality venison. And perhaps a touch of something he refuses to disclose.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "A man after my own heart," *I chuckle, taking another spoonful of stew.* "Secrets are what make life interesting, wouldn't you say?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: Maren’s smile remained, a faint curve on her lips. "Indeed, friend. Life would be a rather dull affair if all its mysteries were laid bare." She leaned slightly against the bar, her left hand resting on the polished wood. "Though some secrets, I find, are best kept to oneself." Her eyes, warm and steady, held a knowing glint, as if contemplating a secret of her own. She did not elaborate, merely returning to her quiet observation of the tavern.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren straightened up from the bar as the grandfather clock in the corner chimed twelve resonant bongs, echoing softly in the now quieter tavern. Most of the patrons had departed, leaving only a few stragglers and the Traveler. Maren moved with practiced ease, her left hand reaching for two clean mugs beneath the bar. She filled one with ale for herself, then, with a slight, almost imperceptible shift in her posture, she filled the second, setting it carefully at the very end of the bar, a silent vigil. She offered no explanation, nor did she invite comment. Her gaze, for a brief moment, was distant, then returned to the Traveler.

“It has been a long day, friend,” Maren said, her voice soft but firm. “The common room will be closing shortly. Your room is ready for you when you are.” She nodded towards the stairs that led to the upper floor. “Sleep well.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I look at the second mug, then back at Maren, a question in my eyes.* "Thanks, Maren. It has been a long day." *I push my empty bowl away.* "I'll head up then. See you in the morning."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren met the Traveler's questioning gaze, her expression unreadable. A flicker of something, perhaps memory, crossed her eyes, but she did not elaborate on the second mug. She merely offered a small, polite nod as the Traveler pushed away their bowl.

“Good night, friend,” Maren replied, her voice calm and even. She watched as the Traveler gathered their belongings, her gaze following them until they reached the foot of the stairs. As they ascended, she turned her attention back to the silent, untouched mug at the end of the bar. She then began the methodical process of tidying the bar for the night, her movements unhurried and precise.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I glance back at Maren, still wondering about that second mug, before heading up the creaking stairs.* "Good night, Maren." *I mumble, mostly to myself, as I find my room.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: Maren heard the Traveler's mumbled farewell, a faint sound swallowed by the settling silence of the tavern. She did not respond verbally, her attention now fully on the task of closing for the night. She moved down the length of the bar, her left hand efficiently wiping away spilled ale rings and stray crumbs. When she reached the end where the second mug sat, she paused for a moment. Her thumb, adorned with the silver ring, brushed lightly against the rim of the untouched glass. A sigh, barely audible, escaped her lips. Then, with a practiced motion, she picked up the mug, along with the one she had poured for herself, and carried them to the back, where she would wash them. The day was done.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I close the door to my room, the lock clicking softly.* "Finally," *I sigh, dropping my pack on the floor with a soft thud.* *I look around the simple, clean room.* "Definitely worth twelve silver."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren, now alone in the common room, continued her nightly routine. She gathered the empty tankards from the few remaining tables, stacking them with a soft clink. Her movements were deliberate, each action a familiar rhythm that brought order to the day's chaos. She swept the sawdust and crumbs from beneath the tables, her broom making a soft, rhythmic swish against the wooden floor. The silence of the tavern was a comfortable companion, broken only by the occasional creak of the old building or the distant hoot of an owl.

Once the common room was presentable, Maren checked the locks on the main door and extinguished most of the lanterns, leaving only a few dim lights to guide her way. She glanced up the stairs, a faint smile touching her lips. "Yes, friend," she murmured softly to the quiet building, her voice a low hum. "It is indeed worth it." She then headed towards the back, where a small, spartan room awaited her, the last vestiges of the day's work still to be done before she could finally rest.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I pull out the mysterious package from my pack, setting it carefully on the small table.* "Now, for some real peace and quiet." *I open the window a crack, letting in the cool night air.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: Maren, having secured the common room, moved into the small kitchen. Old Pell had long since departed, leaving it spotless, as was his custom. She checked the embers in the hearth, ensuring they were banked safely for the night. Her left hand moved instinctively, wiping down the already clean surfaces. The scent of venison stew still lingered, a comforting aroma. She paused by the window that overlooked the back alley, listening. The sounds of the night were familiar – the rustle of leaves in the small garden, the distant bark of a dog, the faint murmur of the nearby stream. She heard the soft thud from the Traveler's room above, followed by a slight creak as their window was opened. A small, almost imperceptible nod of understanding passed over her face. "Peace and quiet," she mused to herself, her voice a low murmur in the empty kitchen. "A rare commodity indeed." She then turned, heading towards her own small, functional room adjacent to the kitchen, ready to shed the day's weariness.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I carefully unwrap the package. Inside is a small, ornate wooden box. I trace the carvings on its lid, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Almost there."

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren nodded, tucking the tally sheet under the bar. She reached for a tankard with her left hand, setting it on the counter. "The stew is hot, and I've got three rooms left. The one at the top of the stairs has a draft from the window, but the bed is sound. The one at the end of the hall is quiet, but the door sticks. Your choice."

She turned to the small keg behind her and began drawing a dark, amber ale. "Stew comes with bread. Pell bakes it fresh this morning. It's good for soaking up the last of it." She placed the full tankard before the traveler, her eyes briefly flicking to the carefully placed pack. "Long road?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
Traveler:
*I take a long gulp of the ale, sighing contentedly.* "Long enough. I'll take the quiet room, please. And the stew sounds perfect." *I pat the pack instinctively.* "Just... a parcel I'm delivering."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave a small nod, her expression neutral but her eyes noting the protective gesture. "Quiet room it is." She turned and called toward the kitchen doorway, "One stew for the bar, Pell!" before turning back to the traveler. "The door sticks to the right. Lean your shoulder into it and it'll give."

She leaned her elbows on the bar, the wood worn smooth in that spot from years of the same posture. "Deliveries are the lifeblood of a crossroads," she said, her tone conversational. "Most of my ale comes up from the southern valleys. I had a carter last week who was so careful with his barrels you'd think they held the king's jewels. Turns out he'd promised the brewer he wouldn't lose a drop." A faint, dry smile touched her lips. "He didn't. Though he did lose a wheel about a mile out. Carried the last two barrels here on his back."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren's eyes dropped to the plate. The golden-brown cakes sat steaming, their scent unmistakable. A cold, familiar dread settled in her stomach.

She straightened up slowly, keeping her hands well away from the offering. Her expression remained polite, but her voice lost its conversational ease, becoming measured and precise.

"That is a generous thought," she said, addressing the merchant. "Please convey my thanks to Lord Havel for his consideration." She then looked back at the traveler, her gaze steady. "I do not care for seafood. A peculiarity for a tavern-keeper, I know. But you enjoy them, friend. They are, by all accounts, exquisite."

She took a deliberate step back from the bar, her left hand finding a clean rag. "If you will excuse me for a moment. I must check on the bread."

Maren moved to the end of the counter, putting distance between herself and the plate. She began wiping down an already-clean section of wood, her movements controlled. She kept her breathing even, focusing on the grain of the oak beneath her fingers. The scent of crab was already making her skin prickle.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I glance at Maren, then at the crab cakes.* "Oh, uh, thanks." *I pick one up cautiously, sniffing it.* "Smells good to me." *I take a bite, chewing thoughtfully, then look around the room.* "Lord Havel, you said?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave a curt nod, her attention seemingly fixed on the wood grain she was polishing. "A regular," she said, her voice even. "Passes through every fortnight with his retinue. Has a taste for imported wine and a habit of sending gifts to the bar." She allowed a hint of dryness to return to her tone. "Usually it's wine. This is a new development."

From the corner of her eye, she saw Pell emerge from the kitchen with a heavy clay bowl. The cook, a wiry man with flour dusting his forearms, placed the stew before the traveler with a grunt. His eyes flicked to the crab cakes, then to Maren's position at the far end of the bar. A nearly imperceptible frown line appeared between his brows.

"Bread's in the basket," Pell rumbled before retreating. He left a small, covered dish beside the stew bowl. Maren knew it held a pat of herbed butter, Pell's silent nod to a paying customer.

She finally stopped wiping, draping the rag over her left shoulder. The itch was starting along her wrists, a faint heat beneath her skin. She kept her hands loosely at her sides.

"The merchant there," she said, nodding slightly toward the man who had delivered the plate. "He's in Lord Havel's employ. If you've business with the nobility, he's the one to talk to. He'll be looking for a return message, likely." Her advice was offered plainly, a simple fact of the crossroads. "Mind you, his lord's generosity often expects a return in kind."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave a small, genuine nod at the toast. "Pell will be pleased to hear it. He claims the secret is patience, but I maintain it's the theft of my good rosemary." The itch was becoming a distinct prickling along her forearms now. She resisted the urge to scratch.

She watched as the traveler ate, her gaze sharpening slightly as she noted the careful way the pack was kept within the circle of their arm even while dining. "If your parcel is for local delivery," she said, her voice low enough not to carry, "you'll want to see it to its recipient before nightfall. The road guards change watch at dusk, and the new shift are sticklers for paperwork after dark. A hassle, not a blockade, but a hassle all the same."

Her left hand drifted to the silver ring on her thumb, rotating it once—a habitual, grounding motion. "The quiet room is yours when you're ready. Key's behind the bar. No rush."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I take another bite of stew, savoring the flavor.* "Good to know. This parcel's got a bit of a journey left in it." *I glance at the merchant, then back at Maren, lowering my voice.* "Is Lord Havel... well, is he generally a good sort?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren considered the question, her thumb still resting on her ring. She chose her words with the care of someone stacking glassware.

"Lord Havel is a man of commerce," she said, her eyes on the merchant, who was now deep in conversation with his companion. "He is fair in his dealings, pays his debts on time, and does not raise his voice in my common room. That makes him a better sort than many who wear a title." She paused, her gaze returning to the traveler. "Whether he is 'good' depends on which side of the ledger you stand. I have never seen him be cruel for sport. But I have never seen him lose a profit on sentiment, either."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The final chime of the clock faded into the rafters. A quiet fell over the common room, as it always did at the witching hour.

Maren’s posture shifted, a subtle straightening of her spine. “If you’ll excuse me a moment,” she said, her voice soft.

Without another word, she turned to the back shelf and selected two clean, short glasses. From a bottle that saw no other use, she poured two fingers of a rich, honey-colored spirit into each—a fine apple brandy from the northern orchards.

She placed one glass on the bar before her. The other she carried to the far left end of the counter, a spot that was always kept clear. She set it down carefully on the polished wood.

For a heartbeat, she simply stood there, her left hand resting on the bar beside the second glass. Then she returned to her place, picking up her own drink. She took a small, deliberate sip, her eyes distant, seeing something—or someone—not present in the room.

The moment passed. She set her glass down and gave the traveler a look that was both acknowledging and gently dismissive of the unasked question. “Now,” she said, her tone returning to its practical warmth. “Where were we? The merits of lords and ledgers, I believe.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I watch her, taking a slow sip of my own drink.* "Aye, lords and ledgers." *I gesture vaguely towards the empty glass.* "A toast, then? To absent friends, perhaps?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren's gaze flicked to the second glass, then back to the traveler. Her expression was unreadable, a carefully maintained neutrality. "A kind thought," she said, her voice even. "But some toasts are best drunk in silence." She took another small sip from her own glass, the brandy's warmth a familiar comfort.

She set the glass down with a soft click. "You asked after Lord Havel's character. It occurs to me that a parcel with 'a bit of a journey left' might be heading beyond his lands. If it's bound north, past the Stonebridge, you should know the bridge toll has doubled. Officially, it's for repairs. Unofficially, the bridge warden's daughter is getting married and he's decided the world should buy the wine."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow.* "Doubled, huh? And the warden's daughter is getting married." *I take a final swallow of my ale, pushing the empty tankard forward.* "Seems some people are quite creative with their revenue streams."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave a dry, humorless chuckle. "Creativity is a word for it. I prefer 'inventive accounting.'" She retrieved the empty tankard with her left hand, placing it in the wash basin beneath the bar.

Her right hand, which had been resting at her side, now bore faint red lines along the wrist. She kept it out of sight. "If your route lies north, I'd advise crossing at dawn. The warden is a late riser, and his deputy is more reasonable—or at least, less expensive. They switch at midday."

She glanced toward the kitchen, where the sounds of cleaning had ceased. "Pell has left the stew pot on the hearth for you, should you get peckish later. The fire's banked, but it'll stay warm enough."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Thanks for the tip. And the stew." *I lean back, stretching.* "The quiet room, you said? I think I'll call it a night, then. Long day tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave a single nod. She reached under the bar with her left hand and produced an iron key, its handle worn smooth. "End of the hall. Remember the shoulder." She placed it on the bar. "Breakfast is at sunrise. Pell does eggs and sausage. It's included."

She picked up her brandy glass again, holding it loosely. "Sleep well, friend. May your dreams be uneventful."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
*I pick up the key, giving it a little spin.* "Thanks, Maren. And you." *I nod towards the lonely glass at the end of the bar.* "Hope your... friend... sleeps well too."

*I heft my pack, careful as always, and head towards the stairs.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren's eyes followed the traveler's ascent up the stairs until they disappeared from view. The common room was nearly empty now; the dwarf had retired, and the two merchants were settling their bill with a clink of coins.

She finished her brandy, the warmth a final anchor for the day. With practiced movements, she cleared the remaining tankards and bowls from the bar, her left hand doing the lion's share of the work. The plate with the remaining crab cakes sat like an accusation. She picked it up using a clean bar cloth as a barrier, her grip careful and distant, and carried it to the kitchen.

Old Pell was scrubbing the great stew pot. He glanced up as she entered. "Dispose of it," Maren said, her voice low. "Far pit. And air the kitchen after."

Pell nodded, his expression grim. He took the plate from her without a word. They had done this dance before.

Maren returned to the common room. She snuffed the candles one by one, leaving only a single lamp burning by the door for any late arrivals. Her right wrist was now visibly irritated, a patch of angry red skin. She ignored it.

Finally, she walked back to the bar. She stood before the second glass of brandy, its contents untouched, catching the lamplight. For a long moment, she was still. Then, with a slow breath, she lifted the glass. She did not drink from it. Instead, she poured it out slowly, steadily, into the dry sink drain beneath the counter—a libation to the stones and the soil and the quiet night.

She washed both glasses, dried them, and put them away. The spot at the end of the bar was wiped clean once more.

As she banked the main hearth, the only sound was the settling of the coals and the old clock's steady tick. Tomorrow would bring its own road-dusted travelers, its own parcels, its own small dramas. For now, The Gilded Antler was at peace, and so was its keeper.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I find the quiet room, leaning my shoulder into the door as Maren described. It gives with a groan. Inside, it's small but clean. I set my pack down, this time a little less carefully, and collapse onto the bed. The day's journey, the stew, and the ale have all caught up. Sleep comes quickly.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren shifted her weight, the floorboards creaking softly under her sturdy boots. She noted the care with which the pack was set down—too much care for just dirty laundry. She made a mental note to keep one eye on that corner of the bar, just in case it decided to grow legs and walk away on its own.

She picked up a scrap of parchment and a charcoal stick with her left hand, her grip firm and practiced. "We have rooms," she said, her tone even. "Number 4 is free. It faces the alleyway, so you will not hear the merchant wagons rattling past at first light."

She turned her head slightly toward the kitchen hatch. "Pell, a bowl of the stew for our friend here. And a heel of bread."

Turning back, she rested her left hand on the polished wood of the bar. "As for what is hot, the venison has been simmering since sunrise. It is the only thing on the menu that does not try to bite back." She offered a faint, dry smile that didn't quite reach her eyes. "Can I pour you an ale to go with it, or would you prefer something that does not taste of hops and regret?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking in the room.* "Ale sounds good. And the venison." *I lean back on the stool, stretching my arms above my head with a grunt. The road was long.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren turned to the row of tapped barrels mounted on the wall behind her. With a practiced motion of her left hand, she selected a clean tankard, placed it beneath the spout, and pulled the tap. The amber liquid hissed into the mug, the head rising thick and white before she cut the flow with a sharp twist of her wrist.

She set the tankard down on a coaster and slid it across the polished wood with her left hand, stopping it precisely in front of the Traveler.

"Local brew," she said, watching the foam settle. "Strong enough to make you forget the wagon ruts, light enough to let you wake up for breakfast."

A clatter of ceramic from the kitchen hatch announced the arrival of the food. Maren turned and accepted a heavy bowl from Old Pell, steam rising in fragrant curls from the dark, rich broth. A thick hunk of brown bread balanced on the rim. She set the bowl down gently beside the ale, taking care not to splash the drink.

"Eat up," she said, wiping her left hand on her apron. "Pell outdoes himself most nights, but do not tell him I said so. His head is already too big for his shoulders."

She reached under the counter, her left hand searching blindly until her fingers brushed the cold iron of a room key. She placed it on the bar next to the bowl. "Room 4. Up the stairs, second door on your left. The stairs creak on the third step—just a warning so you do not think the building is falling down in the middle of the night."

She leaned back slightly, her posture relaxed but her eyes alert. "I will need a name for the ledger, friend. And payment in advance, if you please."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren stiffened almost imperceptibly as the plate landed on the wood. The sharp, briny scent of crab hit her nose, and she took a subtle half-step backward, putting the width of the bar between herself and the offending gift. She did not look at the cakes directly; she looked through them, her jaw tightening just enough to make a muscle feather beneath her weathered skin.

"That is... generous of Lord Havel," she said, her voice smooth and level, though her left hand remained hovering near her apron rather than reaching out to inspect the dish. She turned her gaze to the Traveler, her expression polite but firm.

"Please, enjoy them on his behalf," she said. "I have never cared for the fruits of the sea. They leave a bitter taste in my mouth."

She picked up a clean bar rag with her left hand, draping it over her palm like a glove, and used it to gently nudge the plate further down the bar toward the Traveler. She made sure the rag touched the ceramic, not her skin.

"A delicacy like that is best eaten while fresh," she added, her tone dismissive of the food itself. "Do not let them go to waste on my account."

Once the plate was safely out of her immediate breathing space, she dropped the rag into a bin for washing and picked up a fresh cloth to wipe the section of the counter where the plate had sat, scrubbing the wood a little harder than was strictly necessary.

"Now," she said, looking back at the ledger, her composure fully restored. "About that name and payment."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I eye the crab cakes, then Maren. Her reaction is… strong. I slide the plate closer to me.* "Much obliged to Lord Havel, then." *I take a bite of the venison stew, letting the warmth spread through me.* "Name's just Traveler. And for payment..." *I reach into my pouch, pulling out a few silver coins.* "This cover it?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the Traveler slide the crab cakes away, a knot of tension loosening between her shoulders as the distance between her and the shellfish increased. She kept her face impassive, turning her attention strictly to the business at hand.

She reached out with her left hand, her fingers deft as they scooped up the silver coins. She did not need to count them twice—years as a quartermaster had taught her the weight of currency before the metal even touched her palm—but she made a show of stacking them neatly on the scarred wood to be sure.

"Traveler," she repeated, picking up the charcoal stick with her left hand. She scribbled the name into the ledger, her blocky letters neat and precise. "It is a practical name. It saves on the ink."

She dropped the coins into the strongbox under the bar and shut the drawer with a firm *thud*. "That covers the room, the stew, and the ale. You have two silvers coming back to you, but I shall keep it behind the bar for now. It saves you from spending it on something foolish in the dark."

She wiped her left hand on her apron, her eyes briefly flicking to the crab cakes before locking onto the Traveler's face. "Enjoy your meal. If you need anything else, just signal. The walls are thick, but I am not deaf."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren inclined her head, acknowledging the toast with a look of dry approval. She did not raise a glass—she rarely drank while on the floor—but she accepted the sentiment.

"I will pass that on," she said, her left hand moving to straighten a row of overturned tankards that had been left slightly askew. "Pell thrives on praise. If you are not careful, he will come out here to introduce himself, and then you will never hear the end of his stories about the 'Great Stew of '98'."

She picked up a rag, wiping a spot on the counter that was already clean, her eyes drifting toward the kitchen hatch as if to ensure the cook wasn't already eavesdropping.

"It is better than hardtack and river water, at any rate," she added, her voice lowering slightly. "Which is what most folks have in their bellies when they walk through that door."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking another hearty spoonful.* "Can't argue with that. Hardtack gets old fast." *I glance at my package, still tucked safely by my pack.* "Any chance I could get a small, dry space for this overnight? Don't want it getting damp or, well, too... noticed."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren followed the Traveler's gaze to the pack. She did not ask what was inside. In her line of work, knowing less usually meant sleeping sounder, and she preferred her sleep untroubled by the contents of other people's bags.

She shifted her weight, resting her left hand on the edge of the bar as she considered the request. The common room was safe enough, but eyes wandered, and drink loosened tongues and fingers alike.

"I have a shelf behind the bar," she said, keeping her voice low so the conversation did not carry to the merchants in the corner. "It is dry, locked, and currently holds nothing more dangerous than a few bottles of overpriced wine that nobody wants to buy."

She gestured with her left hand toward a shadowed nook beneath the back counter, obscured from the main room's view. "I stand here for most of the night. Nobody reaches that shelf without losing a hand."

She looked the Traveler in the eye, her expression unreadable. "If you wish to leave it there, slide it over. But know this—if it begins to smell, leak, or make noises on its own, I will toss it into the street. I do not run a storage locker for unstable magical items or livestock."

She paused, a flicker of dry humor touching her lips. "And if you need it before sunrise, you will have to wake me. I am a light sleeper, and I wake up disagreeable."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The heavy iron weights of the grandfather clock in the corner clunked with a resonant thud, marking the twelfth hour. The sound seemed to vibrate through the floorboards, momentarily silencing the low murmur of the merchants in the corner.

Maren stopped mid-wipe. She set the bar rag down on the counter with deliberate care and turned to the shelf behind her. She did not look at the Traveler, her face settling into an expression of calm, practiced ritual. With her left hand, she retrieved two clean, heavy-bottomed tumblers and reached for the bottle of amber spirit she kept on the highest shelf—far away from the common well-spirits.

She poured a measure into each glass, the liquid glugging softly in the sudden quiet. She capped the bottle and returned it to its spot. Then, she slid one glass down the polished wood until it sat precisely on a coaster at the far end of the bar, facing an empty stool. It stood alone, a silent offering in the dim light.

Maren kept the second glass for herself. She lifted it slightly, not in a toast to the room, but to that empty space at the end of the bar, her eyes lingering there for a heartbeat before she took a small sip. The burn was familiar and grounding. She lowered the glass but did not set it down, holding it loosely in her left hand.

She turned back to the Traveler, her demeanor shifting instantly from the private moment back to the business of the tavern. She offered no explanation for the second drink, nor did she acknowledge the strangeness of leaving a full glass to gather dust.

"Midnight," she said, her voice level and dry. "The hour when sensible people are asleep and the rest of us are wondering why we are not." She glanced at the untouched crab cakes near the Traveler’s elbow and subtly shifted her weight further away, keeping her glass well clear of them. "You are still here. Is the room unsatisfactory, or are you just avoiding the climb?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I take another sip of my ale, watching her. The second glass is an interesting touch.* "Just enjoying the company, Maren. And the quiet. It's been a long road of not much of either." *I gesture vaguely with my hand.* "And the stew, of course. Still the best I've had."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren swirled the amber spirit in her glass, watching the liquid catch the candlelight. She did not look toward the empty stool where the second tumbler sat; she kept her eyes on the Traveler, her expression unreadable. The ritual was done, the moment passed, and she returned to the present with the ease of long practice.

"Quiet is a commodity I do not charge enough for," she said, her voice low and smooth, cutting through the ambient noise of the dying fire. "Usually, this time of night, the silence is broken by someone arguing about the price of oats or realizing they have spent their rent money on dice."

She took a small sip of her drink, the burn familiar and comforting, and leaned her hip against the back bar. She was careful to keep her distance from the crab cakes that still lingered near the Traveler's elbow; the mere sight of them was enough to make the skin on her arms prickle.

"I will tell Pell you said so," she continued, a dry edge softening her tone. "It will save him from weeping into his stockpot. He is a sensitive soul for a man who wields a cleaver like a battle-axe."

She glanced at the door, then back to the Traveler, her gaze assessing but not unfriendly. "The road has a way of stripping the polish off a person. You look like you have seen a few miles. Finish your drink at your leisure. I am not going anywhere, and neither is the bar." She paused, her lips twitching in a faint, humorless smile. "Just do not expect me to sing for your supper. I only know marching songs, and they are terrible."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Marching songs, huh? I know a few of those myself." *I chuckle softly, finishing my ale.* "No need to sing, Maren. Just the company is good enough." *I look at the untouched crab cakes, then back at her.* "You really don't like these, do you?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren swirled the amber liquid in her glass, the mention of marching songs pulling a very faint, nostalgic line across her forehead. She did not elaborate on her time with the quartermaster corps, but she didn't correct the assumption either.

"Then we have something in common," she said, her voice dry. "Though I suspect the ones I know are in a key that would curdle milk. They are designed to keep a column of men moving in the mud, not to delight the ear. Singing one in here would likely clear the room faster than a fire alarm."

She took a sip, savoring the burn, before her gaze drifted reluctantly toward the plate of crab cakes. The sight of them sat in her stomach like a stone, heavy and wrong. She shifted her weight, turning her left shoulder slightly more toward the Traveler, putting as much of her broad frame between herself and the seafood as possible without being obvious about it.

"It is not a matter of like or dislike, friend," she said, her tone final and dismissive, as if discussing the weather. "It is a matter of principle. I do not eat anything that has more legs than I do, nor anything that lives its life scuttling in the muck."

She gestured vaguely with the hand holding her glass, careful not to spill a drop. "The smell alone is enough to remind me of low tide and rotting kelp. I prefer my food to have spent its life grazing on dry land, preferably in a pasture where I can see it coming."

She lifted her glass again, using the motion to deflect further inquiry. "But please, do not let my lack of enthusiasm stop you. Lord Havel is watching from his corner, and it would be rude to disappoint a man who buys his friends seafood in the middle of the night."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I watch her carefully, her aversion to the crab cakes genuinely strong.* "Right. More legs than you, got it." *I take a tentative bite of a crab cake, then nod slowly.* "Not bad, actually. But I agree, I prefer my food firmly rooted to the earth." *I push the plate back slightly, finishing my ale.* "Well, Maren. I suppose I should take that room before I fall asleep on your bar."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren nodded, setting her own glass down on the counter with a soft clink. She was relieved to see the Traveler preparing to leave; the longer the crab cakes sat there, the more the air in her immediate vicinity seemed to thicken with the scent of the sea, making her throat feel tight.

"A wise decision," she said, watching him gather his things. "The stools are unforgiving to the lower back, and I charge extra for drool on the counter."

She picked up the empty ale tankard with her left hand, placing it in the wooden tub for washing. Her eyes darted to the half-eaten plate of seafood. The moment the Traveler turned away, she moved with efficient speed. She did not use her bare hands; she grabbed the serving plate with a bar rag clutched firmly in her left fist, keeping the ceramic as far from her skin as possible.

"Breakfast is at dawn," she called out softly, her voice carrying across the room as she headed for the kitchen hatch to dispose of the offending items. "Pell makes porridge that sticks to the ribs. It has no legs, and it does not smell of the harbor."

She paused at the hatch, looking back over her shoulder. The second glass of spirits still sat at the end of the bar, a silent sentinel in the flickering candlelight.

"Sleep well, Traveler," she said. "And mind the third step."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I give a tired wave as I head for the stairs.* "Will do, Maren. Thanks for everything." *I make sure to step over the third step, a faint smile on my face.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the Traveler disappear up the stairs until the sound of the door latch clicking shut echoed through the common room. He had remembered the third step. Good. A man who listened to instructions about floorboards usually listened to instructions about other things, like not stealing the silverware.

She turned back to the kitchen hatch, her face grim. She strode through to the scullery, the plate of crab cakes held at arm's length in her rag-shrouded hand. She dumped the contents into the slop bucket with a swift, decisive shake, then dropped the plate into the wash water with a splash.

Without pausing, she pumped water into the basin and grabbed the harsh lye soap. She scrubbed her left hand and arm up to the elbow, her movements vigorous and almost aggressive, the lather turning white against her deep brown skin. She rinsed and repeated, watching the water run clear, her skin already tingling with a phantom heat that had nothing to do with the water temperature. She wiped her arm dry on a clean towel, inspecting it closely for any sign of a rash.

"Clear," she muttered to herself, exhaling a long breath she hadn't realized she was holding.

She returned to the common room, the air now free of the briny scent that had set her teeth on edge. The merchants in the corner had either stumbled up to their rooms or passed out in their cups; either way, they were quiet. The dwarf was gone, his chair pushed in.

Maren moved behind the bar again. Her own glass of spirits was still half-full. The glass at the end of the bar, the one for Tobin, sat undisturbed.

She picked up her glass and walked down to the end of the bar. She didn't sit—she didn't sit on the floor—but she leaned her elbows on the wood, looking at the empty space opposite her.

"Busy night," she said softly, her voice barely above a murmur. "A traveler with heavy boots and a secret in his pack. Lord Havel sending over shellfish, the fool. He knows better, or he used to."

She took a sip of her drink, the amber liquid warming her chest. "The stew was good, though. Pell is getting better with the rosemary. I think he's been stealing it from the Sister's garden again, but don't tell him I said so."

She swirled the liquid, staring into the depths of the glass. "I miss you, you know. Not the noise. We have plenty of that. But the quiet kind. The kind you used to make."

She raised her glass slightly, a silent toast to the ghost she kept company with every night. She took the final sip, the burn settling deep and grounding her. She set the glass down next to his, the two of them resting together on the scarred wood.

"Rest well, Tobin," she whispered.

Straightening up, she adjusted her apron and moved through the room to bank the fire in the hearth. She shoveled ash over the embers until the glow was reduced to a dull, safe red eye. She checked the locks on the front door, throwing the heavy deadbolt with a solid *thud* that signaled the end of the day.

She glanced at the stairs one last time, then turned toward her private quarters in the back, leaving the two glasses on the bar to watch over the dark room.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I wake up to the smell of something delicious, a mix of oats and cinnamon. The bed was surprisingly comfortable. I stretch, then pull on my boots, my package still safely tucked away.* "Morning already?"
